compatibility.title: Which BMW Models Use the S58B30?
compatibility.intro: The S58B30 is BMW M's flagship straight-six, introduced in 2019 and fitted exclusively to M-division models. It replaced the S55 in the M3/M4 and brought M power to the X3 and X4 for the first time. The engine is offered in multiple states of tune, with the S58B30O0 powering base manual models and the S58B30T0 reserved for Competition, CS, and CSL variants.

costGuide.title: BMW S58B30 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an S58B30 typically takes 16-22 hours at £80-£120/hr (independent M specialist) - the twin-turbo setup, closed-deck block, and complex cooling system make this a significantly more labour-intensive job than a standard B58 replacement.
paragraphs: The biggest price movers for an S58B30 replacement are the condition of the twin turbochargers (OEM replacements are £2,000+ each), the state of the cooling system, and whether the engine is a base 473 hp O0 variant or a 530 hp T0 Competition unit. The cylinder head incorporates 3D-printed core technology - this is not a standard engine to rebuild, and only specialists with M-division experience should be trusted. Post-2022 units with the revised oil pump design and CS/CSL-spec internals command a premium. See our full /prices/reconditioned-engine-cost guide for more detail.

failures.title: BMW S58B30 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Cooling System Leaks - water pump, thermostat housing, and radiator connections
items.whatHappens: The S58 runs hot by design - it has a large central radiator and two smaller flanking radiators plus separate engine oil and transmission fluid coolers. This complex cooling system has multiple plastic fittings and connections that can become brittle over time. The water pump and thermostat housing are known wear points, with coolant loss being the most common early warning. Overheating on an S58 can cause catastrophic damage very quickly.
items.repairVsReplace: Water pump and thermostat replacement is a specialist job (£600-£1,200) given the engine's tight packaging. If the engine has been overheated, head gasket failure may write off the unit entirely - replacement is the only safe route. → Read our full /failures/coolant-system-failure guide

items.title: PCV Valve / Valve Cover Failure
items.whatHappens: Like the B58, the S58 integrates the PCV valve into the cylinder head cover - it cannot be serviced individually. When the PCV diaphragm fails, the engine develops a loud whistle at idle (which stops when the oil cap is removed), rough running, increased oil consumption, and potential oil leaks from seals. A stuck-open PCV valve creates a large vacuum leak, leading to poor drivability and potential stalling.
items.repairVsReplace: The entire cylinder head cover must be replaced (£800-£1,500). This is a known design compromise on the S58 and should be budgeted for on higher-mileage examples.

items.title: Turbocharger Wastegate Rattle and Charge Pipe Leaks
items.whatHappens: The S58's twin single-scroll turbochargers (one per three cylinders, supplied by Mitsubishi) feature electronically controlled wastegates. Over time, wastegate bushings can wear, causing a metallic rattle on cold start and part-throttle operation. Charge pipes, intercooler fittings and rubber couplers can also crack or leak under the high boost pressures the S58 runs, causing power loss or inconsistent acceleration.
items.repairVsReplace: Wastegate repair requires turbocharger disassembly or replacement - a significant cost (£1,500-£3,000 per turbo). Charge pipe replacement is more straightforward (£400-£800) but should be addressed promptly.

failures.goodYearsLine: The S58 is widely regarded as one of BMW M's most reliable modern engines, with no widespread catastrophic failures reported like the S55's crank hub issues. The S58 features a solidly forged crank hub with 4-screw fixation, addressing the S55's weakness. Post-2022 units received further refinement; the S58 has proven capable of 700+ hp on stock internals with supporting modifications. Early bearing shell issues affecting some 2021 production cars were addressed by BMW under warranty.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the S58B30
variants.intro: The S58B30 is a Specific engine code covering BMW M's twin-turbo straight-six. Unlike Family pages that cover multiple fundamentally different engines, this page covers the S58 as a single engine family with multiple output tunes. The engine is BMW M's own design, developed from the B58 architecture but featuring significant M-specific hardware. Where to find your engine code: The engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the engine block, visible from the driver's side of the engine bay. It also appears on the V5C registration document under "Engine number" (e.g. S58B30O0xxxxxx or S58B30T0xxxxxx). For BMW models, the VIN decoder will also confirm the exact variant from the vehicle's build sheet. Key S58B30 variants: | Variant | Power | Key Difference | Applications | |---|---|---|---| | S58B30O0 | 473 hp (353 kW) | Base tune, lower boost, paired with 6-speed manual | G80 M3 base, G82 M4 base | | S58B30T0 | 510-530 hp (375-390 kW) | Higher boost, Competition mapping, 8-speed auto, xDrive available | M3/M4 Competition, M3 CS, M4 CSL, X3 M Comp, X4 M Comp | | S58B30T0 (CS/CSL) | 551 hp (405 kW) | Ultimate tune, revised cooling, lightweight internals | M3 CS, M4 CSL | Why fitting the wrong variant matters: While the S58B30O0 and S58B30T0 share the same physical architecture, they have different ECU calibrations, boost levels, and in some cases, different cooling system components and transmission pairings. Fitting a base O0 ECU into a Competition-spec car will result in significant performance loss and potential DME mismatch errors. The CS/CSL variants feature unique internals and cooling - these are not a straight swap into a standard M3 or M4 without supporting modifications. Commonly confused codes: | Engine Code | What it is | Why it's confused | |---|---|---| | B58B30O0 | 473 hp B58 TU used in X3 M40i (2018-2019) | Similar power output but single-turbo, open-deck block, fundamentally different engine | | B58B30M0 | 326 hp B58 used in 540i, 740i | Same displacement but single-turbo, road car spec | | S55B30 | 425-444 hp S55 used in F80 M3 / F82 M4 | Predecessor - different architecture, open-deck, known crank hub issues |

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement S58B30 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used S58B30 can make financial sense for lower-mileage donor engines from accident-damaged vehicles. However, given the S58's high-performance nature and potential for track use, used units must come with full service history and ideally a compression test. Avoid early 2021 production units without documented bearing shell inspection - some early cars were affected by bearing issues, addressed under warranty. Used prices from £6,500-£9,000 reflect the risk; a £10,830 reconditioned unit with warranty is often better value. Link once:

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A properly reconditioned S58B30 addresses the engine's known weak points: new water pump, thermostat, PCV valve/cylinder head cover, timing components, and full gasket set. Given the £10,830-£13,500 supply cost and the high value of S58-powered vehicles (£30,000-£80,000+), reconditioning is the recommended choice for most owners. A 12-24 month warranty provides essential peace of mind on an engine that can cost over £20,000 from BMW new. Link once:

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full S58B30 rebuild is justified for high-value, low-mileage vehicles or where the engine has suffered a specific failure (e.g. overheated, bottom-end damage). An upgraded rebuild should include forged pistons, upgraded rod bearings, and a strengthened oil pump - particularly relevant for owners planning significant tuning (700+ hp builds). Rebuild costs (£13,500-£18,000+) are significant but still well below a new OEM crate engine from BMW (estimated £25,000+). Only M-specialist workshops with S58 experience should be trusted. acceptedAnswer.text: The engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the block, visible from the driver's side - it will read S58B30O0 or S58B30T0. It also appears on the V5C under 'Engine number'. The easiest method is to check your vehicle's VIN using a BMW decoder, which will list the exact engine code from the factory build sheet. O0 = 473 hp, 6‑speed manual (base M3/M4) or 460 hp (G87 M2). T0 = 510-551 hp, 8‑speed automatic, Competition/CS/CSL tune. Fitting a Competition‑spec engine into a base manual car requires ECU and cooling system changes.

mainEntity.name: Is the S58B30 reliable, and what mileage can I expect?

acceptedAnswer.text: The S58 is widely considered BMW M's most reliable modern engine, with many owners reporting 100,000+ trouble‑free miles when properly maintained. The closed‑deck block, forged internals, and 4‑screw crank hub design address the S55's key weaknesses, and the engine has proven capable of 700+ hp on stock hardware. Typical lifespan: 150,000-200,000 miles with proactive maintenance. Replace water pump and thermostat at 80,000 miles. Check PCV system around 70,000-100,000 miles. Full service history is essential - the S58 is not an engine to neglect.
